cases.summary: Long garden-community lease. Entry-purpose list hides a removal right and a repair shutoff; a broad liability limit hides behind 'unless otherwise required by law'.
Eight-unit building. An AS-IS clause removes the repair duty; the deposit deadline sits in a later section; holdover notice is 15 days.
Scanned-looking mid-rise lease (wrapped lines, page headers). Deposit may sit in the operating account, notice counts weekends, a balcony rule bans flags, abandoned-property clause lacks the legend.
Long single-family house lease. Plumbing shift is allowed for a house; 12-hour entry notice, a gag on code complaints, and a water cutoff for unpaid utility bills are not.
Large community lease. Two removal rights hide in the entry-purpose list, a rekey-on-default remedy hides in the default section, plus force majeure and a crime-only disclaimer.
Townhome community lease: 'as is' with no repair duty, 75-day move-out notice, a fee carve-out for any personal-injury claim, and a utility clause 'as permitted by law'.
Month-to-month duplex with addenda. Termination notice 'by the 15th' (about 15 days), a 35-day claim deadline in the deposit addendum, and a disclosure without the statutory notice.
Scanned condo lease. Two-business-day pay-or-quit, repair entry from 7:00 a.m., and a release from all claims buried in an indemnity paragraph; the U.S. flag is expressly allowed.

findings.title: Limit on landlord liability
findings.problem: The lease tries to release the landlord from liability the law imposes. Florida makes this kind of clause void.

span.quote: Unless otherwise required by law, Owner is not liable to Resident, occupants or guests for any personal injury or for any damage to or loss of personal property, from any cause, including fire, smoke, rain, flood, water leaks, hail, lightning, wind, explosions, theft, or the acts of other residents.

findings.suggestedFix: Delete the clause. Each party remains responsible for its own obligations and liability under law.

findings.title: Utility shutoff
findings.problem: The lease lets the landlord interrupt utilities to make repairs or prevent damage. Florida's statute bars any landlord-caused utility interruption and states no repair exception; temporary repair work is commonly treated differently, so a person should check how this clause is used.

span.quote: (f) to interrupt water or electrical service when needed to complete repairs

findings.suggestedFix: Landlord may temporarily interrupt a utility only as reasonably necessary for repairs or emergencies, with advance notice to Tenant when practical, and will restore service promptly.

findings.title: Removing the tenant's belongings
findings.problem: The lease lets the landlord remove the tenant's belongings without a surrender, abandonment or court eviction. Florida prohibits this.

findings.suggestedFix: Landlord may remove Tenant's personal property only after surrender, abandonment, or a lawful eviction.
